hook: At 5M monthly requests, this model favors Lambda Event Arm ($2.13 vs $5.40); at 100M it favors Workers Standard ($51.40 vs $147.80). The result assumes 512 MB, 200 ms elapsed time, 10 ms Workers CPU and unused allowances. It is modeled pricing, not a cross-runtime benchmark.

sections.title: Two vendors, three meters, two definitions of work
sections.content:
Lambda now publishes two price sheets. Event Functions bill requests plus duration in GB-seconds: $0.0000133334 per GB-second on Arm, $0.0000166667 on x86, and $0.20 per million requests. Web Functions bill active CPU at $0.0000276944 per vCPU-second, memory at $0.0000036667 per GB-second for as long as the environment exists, and $0.30 per million requests.

Workers bill one thing that matters: CPU milliseconds, $0.02 per million after 30 million included, plus $0.30 per million requests after 10 million on a $5 plan. No Workers duration/egress charge does not make D1 free: database usage, storage and database-count overages meter separately.

| Meter | Lambda Event | Lambda Web | Workers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests | $0.20/M | $0.30/M | $0.30/M |
| Duration | GB-seconds | memory GB-s, whole life | none |
| CPU | inside duration | $0.0000276944/vCPU-s | $0.02/M CPU-ms |

sections.title: A GB-second is a memory meter wearing a clock
sections.content:
Duration billing multiplies wall time by allocated memory, and both factors are yours to set. A 512 MB function that takes 200 ms bills 0.5 GB × 0.2 s = 0.1 GB-s per request. At 100 million requests that is 10 million GB-seconds, or $133.33 before the allowance on Arm at $0.0000133334.

Workers bills the 10 ms of actual work instead: 100 million × 10 ms = 1,000 million CPU-milliseconds, which is 970 million after the 30 million included, at $0.02 per million CPU-ms = $19.40.

Elapsed duration and active CPU are different inputs. Equal performance across runtimes is assumed here, not measured; CPU changes and shared allowances can change the ranking.

sections.title: This model crosses near 7.45 million requests
sections.content:
Same shape everywhere below: 200 ms duration, 512 MB, 10 ms of CPU, one modeled workload on the quoted Arm rate and Workers Standard. All stated allowances are unused; no cache, retries, taxes, discounts or other service charges are included.

| Requests/month | Lambda Event (Arm) | Workers | Cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5M | $0.80 + $1.33 = $2.13 | $5.00 + $0.40 = $5.40 | Lambda |
| 7.5M | $1.30 + $4.67 = $5.97 | $5.00 + $0.90 = $5.90 | Workers, by 7¢ |
| 10M | $1.80 + $8.00 = $9.80 | $5.00 + $1.40 = $6.40 | Workers |
| 50M | $9.80 + $61.33 = $71.13 | $5.00 + $12.00 + $9.40 = $26.40 | Workers |
| 100M | $19.80 + $128.00 = $147.80 | $5.00 + $27.00 + $19.40 = $51.40 | Workers |

The crossover is a free-tier artefact, not a policy: 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds are free on Lambda, and 30 million CPU-ms are free on Workers. Below roughly 7.45 million requests the Lambda allowance is worth more than the CPU savings. This is not a universal traffic threshold.

sections.title: Lambda's second sheet splits the same request in two
sections.content:
Web Functions are AWS's answer to active-CPU billing, and they price the same 100 million requests differently.

| Line | Lambda Event | Lambda Web | Workers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests | $19.80 | $30.00 | $27.00 |
| Compute | 10M GB-s = $128.00 | 1M vCPU-s = $27.69, 1.296M GB-s = $4.75 | 970M CPU-ms = $19.40 |
| Plan floor | — | — | $5.00 |
| **Total** | **$147.80** | **$62.45** | **$51.40** |

Web Functions bill $62.45 for the same traffic, 42% of the Event price, and still 21% above the Workers bill. The memory meter is why: it bills the environment for its whole life, idle time included, and AWS's own examples quietly assume exactly one environment stays up for the entire month.

sections.title: Where Lambda wins on the same sheet
sections.content:
The free allowance matters: in the stated 512 MB, 200 ms, 10 ms CPU model, 5 million requests cost $2.13 on Lambda and $5.40 on Workers. This assumes the allowances are not already consumed by other workloads.

Lambda supports up to 10,240 MB. Workers CPU limits vary by trigger; do not treat the HTTP limit as universal:

| Workers Paid invocation | CPU limit | Wall-clock limit |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | 30 s default; configurable to 5 min | No hard limit while client connected |
| Cron, interval under 1 hour | 30 s | 15 min |
| Cron, interval at least 1 hour | 15 min | 15 min |
| Queue consumer | 30 s default; configurable to 5 min | 15 min |

Queue wall time is not CPU time. Free and legacy plans have different limits; verify the deployed configuration. AWS integrations such as VPC, IAM, SQS and Kinesis may also outweigh a small compute-price difference.

sections.title: The exit door has a rewrite behind it
sections.content:
Correction, November 14, 2026: the wait-only example accidentally substituted 200 ms CPU for its stated 10 ms. At 10 million requests, Workers remains $6.40, not $44.40; the extra wall time changes Lambda’s duration bill only. Event Arm rates and the crossover assumptions were rechecked on November 14; unrelated AWS claims retain their earlier source check.

Moving runtimes still requires testing APIs, native dependencies, filesystem behavior and state bindings. Check the actual HTTP, Cron or Queue limit rather than assuming every invocation has a five-minute CPU cap.

The estimate covers one workload with available included usage, not a complete application invoice. Storage, queues, databases, retries and migration work can add costs; measure CPU and elapsed duration separately before choosing.

cost_math.label: 100M requests at 200 ms, 512 MB, 10 ms CPU
The same traffic on Lambda Web Functions
cost_math.result: $62.45, 58% below Lambda's own Event price for identical traffic

cost_math.label: Model-specific crossover with unused allowances
cost_math.result: Approximately 7.45M requests for these assumptions, not a general crossover; 5M favors Lambda, 7.5M narrowly favors Workers.

cost_math.label: Wall time rises from 200 ms to 1 s; CPU remains 10 ms
cost_math.result: Lambda rises from $9.80 to $63.13 (+$53.33); Workers stays $6.40. All stated allowances are assumed available; taxes and other services are excluded.

decision_matrix.situation: 5M monthly requests in the stated 512 MB, 200 ms, 10 ms CPU model
decision_matrix.pick: Lambda Event Arm on modeled request/compute cost
decision_matrix.why: With unused allowances, Lambda is $2.13 vs Workers Standard $5.40. The allowance reduces the charge; it does not cover all 5M requests. Recalculate for other traffic and workloads.

decision_matrix.situation: 100 million requests that mostly wait on I/O
decision_matrix.why: The same shape prices at $51.40 against $147.80, because 10 ms of CPU out of a 200 ms request is all Workers meters.

decision_matrix.situation: A function that needs 10 GB of memory
decision_matrix.why: Lambda supports up to 10,240 MB; Workers uses a much smaller isolate memory budget. CPU limits are separate and depend on the invocation type.
Active-CPU billing ignores the wait: AWS's own LLM streaming example prices 5M requests of 3 s at $33.94, against $101.00 as Event Functions.
Workers charges nothing for egress or bandwidth, and static asset requests are free and unlimited.

decision_matrix.situation: SQS, Kinesis, VPC and IAM already wired into the app
decision_matrix.why: The compute line is often the small one; rewriting event sources and IAM to leave AWS costs more than the difference on the invoice.

decision_matrix.situation: A cron job every hour, minutes of CPU each
decision_matrix.why: At an hourly interval, paid Cron permits up to 15 minutes CPU and 15 minutes wall time. The 720-invocation × 180,000 ms example is $5 + (129.6M − 30M) × $0.02/M = $6.992, about $6.99, assuming no other usage or services.

decision_matrix.situation: Traffic so spiky that one environment cannot serve it
decision_matrix.why: Web Functions bill memory for the life of every environment, and the pricing examples quietly assume exactly one environment runs all month.

verdict_summary: In the stated 512 MB, 200 ms elapsed, 10 ms CPU model with unused allowances, Lambda Event Arm is cheaper at 5M requests ($2.13 vs $5.40). Workers Standard is narrowly cheaper at 7.5M ($5.90 vs $5.97), crossing near 7.45M, and cheaper at 100M ($51.40 vs $147.80). Waiting alone does not establish a winner; volume, memory, CPU, billing model and other services change the result.
migration_guide:
Lambda to Workers is a runtime rewrite: the handler becomes a fetch listener, environment variables become bindings, and anything that needs a native module, a spawned process or a writable disk has no equivalent. State moves to Durable Objects or KV, which bill separately.

Workers to Lambda is smaller but not free: package the code, replace KV and Durable Objects with a database, and accept that egress is metered again. In both directions the traffic analysis comes first, because the arithmetic only favours one vendor when you know the request duration and the CPU share of it.

faqs.q: Does no duration charge mean Workers has no execution limit?
faqs.a: No. Standard Workers bills CPU and requests rather than elapsed duration, but trigger limits still apply. Paid HTTP CPU defaults to 30 seconds and can be configured to 5 minutes. Paid Cron CPU is 30 seconds below a one-hour interval and 15 minutes at intervals of at least one hour. Queue CPU defaults to 30 seconds, configurable to 5 minutes; its separate wall-clock limit is 15 minutes.
A second Lambda billing model that charges per request, per vCPU-second of active CPU and per GB-second of memory for as long as the execution environment exists.

faqs.q: What happens if a request waits longer but still uses 10 ms CPU?
faqs.a: In the stated 10M-request paid-plan model with available allowances, increasing wall time from 200 ms to 1 s leaves Workers at $6.40. Lambda Event Arm at 512 MB rises from $9.80 to $63.13. The old $44.40 Workers result incorrectly used 200 ms CPU. These are modeled costs, not measured performance or complete invoices.

faqs.q: Is Workers always cheaper for I/O-heavy requests?
faqs.a: No. In this model Lambda Event Arm costs $2.13 at 5M requests versus Workers Standard $5.40. At 7.5M Workers is $5.90 versus Lambda $5.97. The crossover is near 7.45M only with the stated memory, duration, CPU, prices and unused allowances; it is not a measured performance result or an all-in bill.

tool_a.name: AWS Lambda
tool_a.tagline: Two bills in one product: duration and active CPU
tool_a.db: Event Functions bill duration in GB-seconds; Web Functions bill active CPU plus memory
tool_a.realtime: Free tier 1M requests and 400,000 GB-s; 10,240 MB memory ceiling
tool_a.ai_readiness: Durable functions at $8 per million operations; streaming priced per GB written
tool_a.lock_in: Medium: event sources, IAM and VPC wiring are AWS-shaped
pros: Free tier covers a small service outright: 1M requests and 400,000 GB-seconds each month
Up to 10,240 MB of memory per function, which a V8 isolate cannot match
Event Functions, MicroVMs, Web Functions and durable functions are all one integration
The event-source catalogue is the reason teams stay: SQS, Kinesis and Step Functions in one IAM model
cons: GB-second billing multiplies wall time by memory, so a request that waits still bills
Web Functions fix the wait but bill memory for the life of every environment, idle included
Event requests list $0.20/M versus Workers Standard $0.30/M; allowances and compute determine the total
Data transfer is metered, so a byte-heavy response is a billable event

tool_b.name: Cloudflare Workers
tool_b.tagline: A flat $5 and a CPU meter, with no duration line
tool_b.db: V8 isolates at the edge: CPU time is the only compute meter
tool_b.pricing: $5/mo minimum · 10M requests included then $0.30/M · 30M CPU-ms included then $0.02/M
tool_b.self_host: No managed equivalent; workerd is open source
tool_b.realtime: Paid HTTP: CPU 30 s default, up to 5 min; paid Cron at least hourly: 15 min CPU; Queue CPU up to 5 min, wall time 15 min
tool_b.ai_readiness: D1, Durable Objects, KV, Queues and Workflows meter separately; static assets are free
tool_b.lock_in: Low on compute, higher on state: Durable Objects hold data inside the product
pros: No charge for duration, egress or bandwidth, which removes the line that surprises AWS bills
The $5 plan includes 10M requests and 30M CPU-ms, enough for a real product to start
Ordinary static assets have a free request rule; Workers Caching requests are metered
Workers Caching hits avoid execution CPU but remain billed requests; other cache paths differ
cons: CPU and wall-clock limits depend on trigger and plan; HTTP defaults to 30 s CPU, configurable to 5 min on Paid
The runtime is not a container: native modules, spawned processes and writable disks do not run
Memory is an isolate-sized budget rather than a configurable 10 GB
At very low volume the $5 floor is more than Lambda's free tier charges
